item.title: Book Review: Nexus by Ramez Naam
item.description: Originally submitted to Scott Alexander's book review contest
item.content:encoded:
What kind of science fiction are we living in today?

Ramez Naam’s 2012 novel Nexus is not the answer, but there are some parallels:

  • A breakthrough technology in the 2020-30s has the potential to accelerate scientific progress and improve the human condition, but also to cause tremendous harm.

  • Institutions are increasingly defined by how they balance technological progress with safety.

  • A plucky group of developers in San Francisco recognize the risks but build a vastly more powerful version, believing that the benefits outweigh the harms because the good guys (themselves) will find the right safeguards.

  • A leading developer of the technology named Ilya inexplicably disappears from the action.

  • It is uncertain whether any of this is expected to be a net positive for humanity.

Naam believed that this change was coming. He said that the technological wonders of the next few decades would rival “even the greatest science fiction” and wrote Nexus to prepare readers for the moral and political questions ahead.

Nexus’ achievement is to do this without being reductive. It converts the “safety vs progress” debate into a deeply human narrative that steelmans both sides. I almost cried sympathizing with the pain technology unleashes on Nexus’ protagonists, but I also felt angry when ignorant fears destroyed their chance at a liberating future. Obviously these scenarios are fictional, but feelings are useful information to work through normative issues.

If you spend a lot of time thinking about how society will respond to radical technological change in the near term, you should read this book for its ability to bring these questions to life.  It looks at the fog-of-war of the future and, from a set of assumptions, charts how one possible pathway might feel. Novels can force authors to specify their assumptions and build a “verbal model” of their predictions. While Naam has written some futurist nonfiction, Nexus shines an emotional light on technology in a way that nonfiction just can’t. And while Naam eventually comes around to soft techno-optimism, the book leaves the net harms and benefits as an open question for the reader.

Despite this, Nexus is not our world. Naam was wrong. Wrong about which technologies would take off, who would develop them, how governments would react to these changes, and more. Nexus is a transhumanist story about brain-computer interfaces and biotech, not AI. The technology is developed by grad students in underground hacking communities, with corporations completely absent. The central villain is a supercharged version of the US Government, capable of not only passing constitutional-amendment-level tech regulations, but waging a War on Terror/War on Drugs inspired campaign to enforce them.

It’s fascinating to see an author take such a big swing— pouring his heart into a work of fiction to safeguard the future he thinks is possible— just to have his assumptions fall flat in hindsight. Naam was a futurist who missed AI. Nexus was published two months after AlexNet, but Naam was consistently bearish on AGI, stating that “AI progress has been 20 years away for 60 years,” or that the developers working on AI were “not the ones excited about it.” His own vision of exponential progress in brain-computer interfaces failed to materialize. Neuralink is doing exciting work today, but paralyzed patients first moved a cursor with their minds in 2006. It’s telling that Naam now works primarily on solar energy, where his predictions were more prescient, rather than human enhancement.

Science fiction does not have to predict the future to be valuable. But Naam really thought that Nexus would. The book has an afterword called “The Science of Nexus” making this argument. When asked if science fiction can predict the future in an interview, Naam cited Arthur C. Clarke predicting communication satellites and Jules Verne predicting and even inspiring the submarine. Then, when given a chance to waffle about his own prescience, Naam said that he hopes neuroscientists read his novel to get inspired about avenues of research.

Nexus shows some of the best and worst qualities of fiction as a medium to write about the near future. Charting a path through the fog-of-war is captivating (I couldn’t put the book down) and important for society, but because of this, compelling stories can become blinders. If you think a lot about AGI today, you could also read Nexus as a cautionary tale of getting too emotionally invested in one model of the future. It may be wise to emotionally hedge on a range of possible stories instead.

Lastly, Nexus is just a fun read. Noah Smith called it a “fast-paced thriller with plenty of gun battles and international plots and evil techno-gods vs. peaceful techno-hippie communes and other fun stuff.” This review will argue Nexus still has something to say about our own sci-fi timeline, but I hope it also convinces you to read it for its own sake.

Connecting Minds

In 2040, an illegal drug called Nexus 4 allows users to share information and experiences between minds. In underground raves and secret meditation groups, connection-seekers drink a silvery liquid filled with nanobots that bind to neurons in the brain, wirelessly sending and receiving signals. In response to high-profile terrorist bio-attacks and mind control cults, Congress has empowered an ‘Emerging Risks Directorate’ to wage a full-scale War on Nexus against even these benign use cases. This review will avoid spoilers past the first ~third of the book, though it’s clear throughout that Nexus’ potential is enormous.

The novel’s two protagonists meet at one of the secret “combining consciousnesses” rave/meditation parties. Kaden Lane, a neuroscience PhD student, hosts the party to test his friend group’s new invention, Nexus 5. This upgraded version allows users to run an operating system and write software on their brain to regulate emotions, download information, and more. Meanwhile, Samantha Cataranes, an undercover ERD agent, infiltrates the party to shut it down and bring Kade into custody. Sam embodies the “harms from technology” perspective, with a horrific backstory and fed mentality to contrast against Kade’s optimism.

Kade is an idealistic genius in over his head. Nexus 5 has the potential to change the world, but the book opens with him testing a module to flirt without being awkward and a group psychedelic meditation trip. Still, Kade and his friend group all see Nexus as a way to liberate humanity. One example is Watson Cole, a former US soldier who committed atrocities until he was held in a prisoner-of-war camp and forced to consume Nexus. It connected him with his victims and made him relive their traumas over and over from their perspective. This changed Wats forever, who converted to Buddhism and pledged to spread Nexus for its potential for empathy and peace. Because the technology is illegal, its developers are heroic underground hackers like this. They can’t take the first job offer from Google and corporations can’t shape the story.

In contrast to Kade, Sam is an extremely competent spy with transhumanist body modifications and a cynical worldview. She warns Kade of the unintended consequences and abuse that releasing Nexus 5 would cause. She’s reluctant to even try it, but as the agent with the most reason to distrust Nexus, the ERD chooses her to infiltrate Kade’s orbit. Although she telepathically reveals her identity by accident, Sam and the army of uber-DEA agents successfully capture and blackmail Kade into working for them.

The real drama of the story unfolds when Kade reluctantly agrees and travels to the sexiest sci-fi thriller setting: a machine learning and neuroscience conference. The US government is in a quasi-Cold War with China, who they believe is developing dangerous upgrades to Nexus, human cloning, and intelligence enhancement technologies. Kade and Sam’s mission is to infiltrate a top Chinese scientist’s research team to find out.

AI as we think of it today is basically absent from the story. Software-based AI is confined to narrow task-specific intelligences, like when Sam instructs a “daemon” to alert her if certain conditions in the hotel security system change, or Kade setting up essentially a Google Alert to monitor the web for keywords. Without spoiling specifics, the book is very interested in whole-brain emulation as a path to AGI, but this assumption makes even AI systems extensions of human agency.

Because of this, Nexus has very little to say about technological misalignment rather than misuse. Nexus has no will of its own and always works as a human intends, either its user or a hacker. The book’s catastrophic situations result from people using it badly, not from inherent technical flaws that make it inconsistent with human values. If you are only interested in this distinction as it relates to AI, skip to the section “Is Nexus Really ‘Post-Human’ Tech?”

Nexus’ moral arc is left with:

  1. Technology empowers people to achieve their desires in ways that were not possible before.

  2. Some people use it for selfish, evil, or ignorant purposes, which the government tries to stop.

  3. Others want to use it for noble, altruistic, or harmless ends, but are barred from access.

  4. It’s not clear how to enforce 2 without causing 3.

While our timeline debates these questions in ‘AI Governance’ papers and Marc Andreesen screeds rather than with guns, I think Nexus has a lot to say about this. Naam is at his best when he makes you sympathize with the father of a severely autistic child using Nexus to connect with his son, or the horror of a civilian having their mind/body hijacked in a terror attack. If you think AI has the potential to empower a lot of good and bad actors in the near future, Nexus may resonate with you.

Technological Freedom and Safety

The following argument comes from an early chapter of Nexus, not from an EA forum comment thread with six upvotes:

“How can you be so naive, Kade? You’re a good guy. I've felt that. But what about other people who get their hands on this?” [...]

“This is stupid. You can hurt people with guns. You can get them to do awful things with words. We need this. ‘Our current problems can’t be solved by the level of thinking that created them.’ Einstein said that. This can take us to a new level of thinking.”

“Kade, it’s going too fast. You’re talking about changing everything about people, the way we’ve been for a hundred thousand years, in a heartbeat. You can’t know the consequences, you can’t understand how people will abuse this, you can’t know that humanity will survive this.”

Nexus traces a standard technological “caution” vs “progress” debate. When characters argue for less regulation, they say things like “we don’t have to hand control of our lives to faceless bureaucrats and secret police,” or “broad dissemination and individual choice turn most technologies into a plus. If only the elites have access, it’s a dystopia.”

The book is weakest when it tries to directly reason with you like this. But fiction can do more— it’s one of the reasons I’m glad Scott prioritized non-nonfiction in the book review this year. When it works, a novel or even poetry can let readers defamiliarize settled points of view. Fiction might be the closest thing we have to ‘Nexus’ in real life for feeling the experiences of others.

Nexus is fundamentally about empathy. It’s full of examples of what living with emerging technology might feel like. I was moved when Sam experienced the mind of a child staring at the world with awe and wonder. Her own backstory gives her tremendous reasons to care for children, and re-experiencing these wholesome moments was healing for her. Similarly, Wats’ backstory of reliving his victims’ trauma makes the “empathy” angle quite literal. He calls himself the dark mirror of a bodhisattva, the opposite of an enlightened teacher, as his negative karma and risk of being reborn in hell allow him to liberate others.

As they bond throughout the story, Sam and Kade share memories and hold each other's minds in compassion. They relive each other’s formative moments to see their worldviews from the inside out. I wish I could experience this with my loved ones— to live the memories that made my family who they are, to see my partner’s internal world, to fully know and be known. Nexus’ protagonists imagine a world without miscommunication or hatred, where anyone can be understood if they want to be. 

The positive uses of technology in Nexus are inspiring. Researchers can collaborate telepathically while working on life saving drugs, climate tech, and more, working as one mind with enhanced memory and creativity. Parents can understand their mentally impaired children. Millions could be saved from neurological and mental health challenges. The technology is not widely circulated yet in Nexus, so its protagonists mostly dream about this potential.

When Kade meditates with a group of experienced monks using Nexus, he feels a deep equanimity and unity that could have taken years of practice to reach without it. His experience is liberating, with all attachments dissolving away into a single “now.” Naam writes:

“The minds in the room were a web, a tapestry, an orchestra of thought without thought. The room breathed in. The room breathed out. A thought occurred in the mind of a novice. It rippled across the mind of the room. All observed it. All brought attention back to the breath.”

Afterwards, a monk compares the scale of learning meditation to learning to read— a transformation of his relationship to the world as impactful as literacy. I think some serious meditators would agree with this characterization. The monk asks Kade what life would be like if learning to read took decades of practice, such that only a few experts could do it. He asks, if you could show people a faster way, would you? Even though it would be used throughout history for vile speech, to create tyrannical governments and wars, to empower the slave trade, and worse? Kade (and Ramez Naam) seem to say yes. The book argues that human empowerment results in more good than harm, but only tentatively, with serious trade-offs along the way.

Nexus’ moral arc is that voluntary human connection is intrinsically good. I say voluntary because, when it works, Nexus allows users to turn “off” their connection to others, not sending or receiving any signals that they want to avoid. Yet nefarious hackers find a way around these firewalls. Nexus becomes the highest possible stakes version of cybersecurity, with even a single vulnerability turning you into a puppet or worse. I suspect cybersecurity experts would never use Nexus for this reason. Every system has vulnerabilities, but the book’s techno-optimists seem to think they will figure out how to make Nexus secure… eventually?

They fail in all sorts of disastrous ways. State actors force-feed Nexus to turn people into suicide bombers against the communities they love. People experience deep privacy violations from malicious hackers and the government. The book has some pretty horrific sexual assault references of people losing mental autonomy through technology. Naam will introduce a charming side character that you start to care for, only to show how a bad guy with the right tech can destroy them:

“There were more screams coming from the living room. *** was still alive. He was on fire, burning to death. She felt every moment of it in her mind, felt *** collapse to her knees from smoke inhalation, her lungs burning.”

It’s hard to understand why anyone would risk using Nexus. But if the potential benefits are good enough, Naam thinks people would try despite the legal or technical risks. He argues that making it illegal just moves tech underground and removes the ability to ensure safety standards— a direct anti-War-on-Drugs mentality that may or may not have parallels to open-source AI. Naam argues that once the technology is widely released, there would be no going back to fight it on the supply side.

Some characters in Nexus go so far as to dream of becoming “posthuman,” transcending the limitations of human intelligence and mortality. The word comes up dozens of times in the novel, from regulators outlawing “posthuman” technology to scientists dreaming of a “posthuman” successor to the human race. Still, compared to the possibility of AGI, Nexus is surprisingly prosaic on this in hindsight. There is no non-human agency in the novel.

Is Nexus Really “Post-Human” Tech?

At one point, Naam gestures to the difficulty regular scientists would have understanding the work of posthuman minds. If Nexus users have enhanced memory, concentration, pattern recognition, creativity, etc, they may create updated versions of Nexus beyond normal human comprehension. Regulators could be unable to keep up. The US Government’s leading scientist even warns that “Nexus may defy human understanding because it is not the product of normal human thought.” 

Then this idea is basically… dropped? For the rest of the book? Despite their scientists refusing to use Nexus themselves, the government does learn how to enhance their agents with Nexus 5, including Sam. They use Kade’s tech against one of his friends in a way that he had failed to discover. No post-humans were required for this innovation. And while the developers using Nexus are more prolific, the book doesn’t seem at all interested in whether this could lead to exponential improvements or an intelligence explosion. The story centers around distribution and incremental improvements to Nexus 5, a potential blindspot in Naam’s worldview.

To be clear, not every book needs to be a “line go up” AI analogy, especially not in 2012, but recursive improvement is a weird omission in a story about enhancing intelligence. It fits with the novel’s broader disregard for technological risks beyond just a bad guy with access.

Nexus is complementary to human agency in a way that artificial intelligence might not be. The tech has no will of its own, cannot replicate or act without a human brain, and rarely even malfunctions. There is no pre-deployment safety standard— Kade sometimes pushes updates that have not been tested straight to prod on his own brain. Nexus is all about misuse, not misalignment. How alignment plays out in real life with AI will be an empirical question, but as a verbal model of one possible future, Nexus totally misses the possibility. Nexus may be disanalogous to AGI because it does not need to be carefully aligned to its users values.

Nexus is also not interested in narrative factors beyond human agency. The story is driven by its characters’ heroic choices rather than structural forces. There are no economic incentives pushing development in a certain way. PhD students just tinker out of passion, not even complaining about UCSF granting decisions. Nexus portrays geopolitical incentives between China and the United States naively, with the US disregarding economic growth and China disregarding social disruption from tech. Eventually, every major character in Nexus turns into a countercultural renegade against their institutions, rather than pulled into their orbit. Even the US government is portrayed as a cartoonish array of selfish generals and ambitious leaders, with a few edgy scientists resisting from within.

Don’t get me wrong, this makes for a gripping narrative! Human agency is really exciting. Naam has described Nexus as an “X-Men like story” of empowered individuals against a distrustful society, and notes that he chose to make the technology illegal in part because “it’s more fun.” I stayed up late reading Nexus to see what would happen. But all of this reveals why inherently misaligned technology impacting the world is hard to write about. 

AGI x-risk people are constantly critiqued for relying too much on science fiction, but I wish more authors would concretize their predictions in fiction. Even Naam, an explicitly futurist author who worked for “Singularity University” and wrote fiction about radical new technology coming after 2012, missed AI. Verbal models of the future can reveal an author’s underlying assumptions. I would like to read a near-future “man vs. shoggoth” story on Nexus’ emotional level. We don’t have too much “posthuman” near-future science fiction, we have too little.

Does Fiction Help Us Think About the Future?

It’s easy to forget what a strange and courageous thing it was to be a “futurist” in the early 2000s. Serious Journalists would scoff at claims that radical change was coming. The idea that a machine could “imitate intelligent human behavior” lived on websites that looked like this. Fiction was a way to talk about this stuff without getting weird looks. “It’s just a story.”

Now, it feels like everyone is a futurist. New York Times columnists have takes on scaling laws. My barber asked what my AI timeline was. Any moment, my grandma will be asking how tensor factorization impacts the robustness of episodic memory.

Naam was working through a set of “if…then” assumptions about the near future and taking their conclusions seriously at a time when this was hard. He took a big swing and even got the scale of the transformation right. Fiction allowed him to reach a wider audience, to bring an emotional depth that nonfiction couldn’t, and to concretize his assumptions. Did he get some things wrong? Absolutely. But Naam is humble about his mistakes. In a 2022 interview with Noah Smith, he said:

“As forecasters, it’s absolutely essential that we actually look at what we predicted and see what we got right and got wrong. [...] On human biology? On life extension? On brain augmentation? I was wrong.”

I was harsh about this, and about AI’s omission from Nexus, but science fiction is worth defending. It has taken a weird beating from the left for supposedly empowering right-wing billionaires and from the right for supposedly empowering decel fears. I’m not sure either of these things is really true, and I’d much rather have a series of weird possible futures to think about than to demand that it will be prosaic. More writers should build verbal models of the AGI near-future for their readers, ideally multiple.

Nexus is also still worth reading within the overton window of AI debates today. Most of the legislation proposed in Congress and the EU centers around harms from AI caused by humans. Even the “Frontier AI Regulation” paper written by everyone mostly focuses on risks to public safety via misuse, such as disinformation, cyberattacks, and biological weapons. The way Nexus makes you feel about these issues in general could be useful information for taking normative positions, or for thinking about how to persuade others.

I hope readers of this review give Nexus a try. I also hope it spurs a conversation about what other near-future fiction is worth reading. If disruptive change is likely to happen in my lifetime, what should I read to emotionally hedge on a bunch of possibilities? The Lifecycle of Software Objects? It Looks Like You’re Trying to Take Over the World? I’d love to hear some suggestions.

item.title: My Notes from 'So Good They Can't Ignore You' by Cal Newport
item.description: Obsessive improvement at an in-demand skill set beats "finding your passion"
item.content:encoded:
Cal Newport's So Good They Can't Ignore You is a fantastic 50 page book stretching out to fill 300 pages. To be fair, most of the advice genre has this 80/20 ratio of value/content (including The 80/20 Principle itself), and I think Cal Newport would even agree. He'd want you to get on to more important work once you've bought the argument.

This post is my attempt to distill So Good They Can't Ignore You so that when I tell people "you should obsessively improve at an in-demand skill set in a legible way" I can point them here. If anyone has told you to develop "career capital" this is also the book that popularized the term.

In short, passion is overrated for developing an enjoyable and impactful career, but thinking like a craftsman who gains valuable skills and assets is underrated. As you become "so good they can't ignore you" you can leverage the career capital you develop to do more impactful work, gain autonomy, work on creative projects, etc. Passion will follow.

This is not a full review of the book, just notes from what I found useful. This post (and everything on my blog) is a reflection of my personal views, not those of my employer. While Cal Newport is interested in how to have a career you enjoy, I think these principles strongly apply for using your career to maximize social impact, which you should do.

"Follow Your Passion" is Bad Career Advice

The things that make a job fulfilling or impactful are rare and valuable. If you want them in your life, you need something rare and valuable to offer in return. You need to be good at something before you can expect a good job.

This might sound obvious, but Newport shows that even you, smart reader of books, are probably overestimating passion and underestimating expertise. It’s everywhere in our culture. Steve Jobs' "follow your passion" Stanford commencement address has 45 million views, yet if Steve Jobs had followed his passion as a young man, he would've been a Zen teacher in Los Altos. Instead, he noticed that he had something valuable to offer the consumer electronics industry and made a series of bets to capitalize on that skill. He got really good, and passion followed from the many other benefits of that decision.

A big part of this problem is that it’s really hard to know a priori what types of work you would enjoy. It’s even harder to predict what you will excel at and how success will improve your enjoyment of the work before you try. We just aren't exposed to a very big sample size of "passions" early in life compared to the vast range of valuable skills we could offer the world. And for supply and demand reasons, the easy-to-find-passion skills aren’t likely to overlap with the rare and valuable skills.

Lastly, your mental model of passion may just have causality backwards. I loved performing live comedy when I was in high school, but if I’m honest with myself, the feedback loop was much more like “Skill → Passion” than “Passion → Skill.” It’s always going to be a mix of both, but we tend to underrate the former, and to underrate passion’s elasticity in general. 

Thankfully, there are many rare, in-demand skill sets with positive feedback loops in the labor market.

A Tale of Two Marketing Executives

Newport fills the book with anecdotes and stories to pad out each chapter. These might help some readers learn from examples, but I think only one encapsulates his worldview enough to warrant including in detail here.

One marketing executive, Lisa Feuer, hates the corporate grind but is passionate about yoga in her free time. She quits her job to take a one month yoga teaching program. Loving it, she re-mortgages her house to open her own yoga studio and live her entrepreneurial dream. Her yoga studio fails and the story ends with her waiting in line for food stamps.

Another marketing executive, Joe Duffy, hates the corporate grind but has been told he's pretty good at making logos for clients. Responding to this feedback, he works hard to improve and build relationships, doing more direct illustrations for corporate clients. He becomes obsessive about his work, landing clients like Coca Cola and Sony, and gets known as one of the best in the industry. Because he is so valuable, he’s able to extract more free time, autonomy, and creative control to work on projects he enjoys. He eventually launches his own firm, whose success allows him to purchase a hundred-acre cross country ski resort at 45 years old and pursue a passion for skiing in his now-abundant leisure time.

If he was passionate about yoga, I’m sure he could have done that as well.

Of course, one anecdote isn't proof of Newport's worldview. It could have gone differently for Feuer or Duffy, and there's no way of knowing whether Lisa would have found success or fulfillment staying in marketing. Joe’s path was also quite difficult, involving sacrifices along the way.

Still, the story is illustrative of Newport’s thesis. Rather than quitting the industry and burning  his existing career capital, Duffy developed and strategically invested it. Teaching yoga is a less rare and in-demand skill, it’s harder for new entrants to break into, and Feuer had almost 0 experience to leverage as a comparative advantage. It's really difficult to find a rare and valuable job without rare and valuable assets to offer in return.

Maybe you find this story a little mean-spirited or stuck up. You might think Joe just became a stuffy corporate shill, bootlicking to the free market or whatever. Cal Newport doesn't care that you think that. He's interested in what makes people’s careers happy and impactful, and Joe’s career exceeded Lisa’s in that regard. Joe was able to carve out ownership, autonomy, and creative control by getting really good.

Plus, even if you don't value traditional metrics of success, being really good at something allows you to negotiate for whatever you value. Better work life balance to practice yoga in your free time? High-impact charity work? Once you can demonstrate that you have rare and valuable skills, you can leverage them for a range of outcomes. What would it mean in your field if you were among the best in the world at what you do? You should be more ambitious about this.

How to Get Really Good and Make People Notice

Once you agree with the book’s framework, the rest is mostly standard career self-help and positive psychology stuff. I'm going to include the examples or concepts I did find personally helpful, but I expect we've covered 50% of the value of the book already.

If you don't already have them, you should mentally download a few examples of successful people close to your field who worked really hard, compounded that effort, and achieved world-class results. Newport offers a few that I liked.

Ira Glass, host of This American Life, obsessively focused on improving his skills in an industry where "the tape doesn't lie." That is, radio producers have a finished product to present that relies on a specific set of measurable skills. Obviously Newport and myself are not asserting that radio or any other field is a perfect meritocracy, but it's useful to focus on what you can control. Ira Glass spent many years on prosaic skills like tape cutting and interviewing to position himself as someone useful at a junior level on an NPR show, then worked up.

When Ira Glass gives career advice, he emphasizes that it takes time to get good at anything, recounting the many years it took him to master radio to get interesting options. “The key thing is to force yourself through the work, force the skills to come; that’s the hardest phase,” he says. Work is hard, so suck it up.

Glass says that “in the movies there’s this idea that you should just go for your dream, but I don’t believe that. Things happen in stages.” When a young person pushed him for more concrete plans, he pushed back: “I feel like your problem is that you’re trying to judge all things in the abstract before you do them. That’s your tragic mistake.” It's hard to know a priori what we will be good at or enjoy.

The comedian Steve Martin used a similar approach. The phrase "So Good They Can't Ignore You" comes from his approach to succeeding in comedy. Martin says nobody wants his career advice, because they'll ask how to get an agent or how to promote themselves, and he'll tell them to go work on their set.

By his own estimation, Martin spent ten years refining his act. At a time when standup was almost entirely cliche setup and punchlines, Martin asked “What if there were no punchlines? What if there were no indicators? What if I created tension and never released it? What if I headed for a climax, but all I delivered was an anticlimax?” He worked in clubs for little pay or acclaim for years, seeking tons of feedback to iterate on a genuinely rare and valuable skill.

So you need to practice, but how? Newport uses the term "deliberate practice" to describe the combination of strain and feedback that allows excellent performers to improve quickly. The number of hours you practice is important, but if you aren't practicing at the edge of your comfort zone— if it doesn't feel like hard work— you aren't going to improve very quickly. The best musicians obsessively play the same riffs over and over. And, if you don't have built in feedback loops— mentors, readers, regimented test materials, whatever— you won't know when you've gone astray and wasted an hour of practice.

Deliberate practice will be specific to your field, but you should think hard about how to develop the habit. As Tyler Cowen often asks, "What is it you do to train that is comparable to a pianist practicing scales?" Even knowledge workers should have an answer to this question. Here is Tyler's. What is yours? If you’re a writer, you should be sharing drafts with people often, looking for comments on blog posts or forums, and inviting harsh feedback from mentors. If you’re a coder, you should have an impressive GitHub, contribute to open-source projects, and use your job to learn a bunch of new stuff. Consider this an invitation to shake off your complacency.

It's also important to tailor your career capital to your specific field. Not all fields are "winner take all" skill markets like stand up comedy. Newport uses this term to mean fields where a single skill dominates all others, such as writing. He says many other fields are "auction markets," such as investing or consulting, where the combination of several skills and networks combine to form career capital. I'd encourage making a list of the skills you respect from high profile peers or mentors, and asking which are mission-critical. Assets like a social network are part of career capital, but are still downstream of skills like sociability. You can get better at parties.

A Bunch of Important Caveats:

  • Personal fit for a job still matters a lot, and passion can be part of that. If there is something that you love to do that other people find to be exhausting work, that's an amazing signal for a rare high value skill. Just don't expect to know this entirely ahead of time - take a series of small bets to try stuff out.

  • Working hard and practicing deliberately should include avoiding burnout. If you work yourself sick and quit at something after a month, you're not actually developing long-term career capital. Take care of yourself.

  • Similarly, beating yourself up because you're not in the top 1% of performers is probably counterproductive. Comparisons should be time-bounded (what was x person doing at my age/experience level) and action-relevant (don’t ask "what if I was an entirely different person?")

  • Some jobs don't actually have opportunities to distinguish yourself by developing and showcasing skills. It’s possible you work somewhere with 0 interest in your career capital. Talk to lots of people to determine whether this is the case, but if it is, look for the exit. This is not somewhere you want to stay.

  • Similarly, if your job forces you to work with people you actively dislike, or to do something you think is evil, you should leave.

  • Deliberate practice can take place in your free time, but ideally it should also be through your 9-5. You spend a huge chunk of your time there and it’s likely the main way you can demonstrate these skills. You should aim for internships, fellowships, education, or jobs that have a lot of feedback from mentors and opportunities to actually improve at important skills.

  • Luck is a big factor in people's careers, such as meeting the right person at the right time, but you can increase your "luck surface area" by putting yourself out there more. Let everyone in your field know that you work hard and want to contribute. Go to conferences. Start a blog. Send cold emails to people whose work you respect.

Leverage Your Career Capital to Make the World a Better Place and Enjoy the Ride

Career capital will come with many benefits. You’ll be offered more opportunities, better financial compensation, and cushy rewards to try to keep you on. But it's important not to fall into the trap of merely following conventional "success." Once you are a valuable asset, you should negotiate for what is actually important. It's not enough to just have skills, you need to leverage them effectively.

Newport makes a convincing case that you'll be happier if you push for creative control and autonomy in your field, even if it means turning down a promotion or having difficult conversations with your boss. Once you are valuable enough that they don't want to lose you, you can push for more impactful work, more exciting projects, or you can walk away to build your own thing, all of which Joe Duffy did. I’m a pretty agreeable person by nature, but this is an important place to be willing to be disagreeable and advocate for yourself. The path that is best for your career won’t be the path that is best for your employer forever.

So Good They Can’t Ignore You ends with a meandering section about how your career should be a "mission" so that your life has a meaningful purpose. It's all super vague. Newport's best example is of a TV show personality whose show was canceled right after the book came out, and he admits that he personally doesn't even have a career mission yet. I imagine the publisher wanted this in the book, or Newport knew he needed a big picture note to end on.

The self-help and career genre has little to offer here. These are big questions. What is this all for? What obligations do we have toward the suffering of others, and how can my vocation contribute in a way that feels personally meaningful? These are better suited to philosophers than to career advice bloggers.

Thankfully, a lot of really smart philosophers have thought about this problem. I find the answers that formed the effective altruism movement quite convincing. Not everyone is lucky enough to be in the position you are now. The global poor, unfathomable numbers of suffering animals, and future generations are crying out for your help. Now that you have rare and useful skills, you can use them to make the world a better place. This is really exciting! I expect it will feel really good, and you should try it out to see for yourself.

Many jobs that are rewarded by the market don’t contribute to solving the world's most important problems and maximizing social impact. But there are resources to think about which ones do. I'd encourage you to consider how your skills can contribute to the career paths that best contribute to reducing harm, improving wellbeing, and saving lives at the margin. I recommend 80,000 Hours' career guide as a great place to start.

item.title: The Eldritch Horrors of Cat vs. Human vs. AI Intelligence
item.description: What Unknown Unknowns Will Also Scale With Intelligence?
item.content:encoded:
I know many things that my cat does not. She understands that her food comes from cans in the kitchen, but not that it comes from a manufacturing plant a thousand miles away. When she wants more, she successfully predicts that she can get it by yelling at me, but not that she could exchange her labor to purchase hundreds of cans.

When AI researchers talk about "cat-level intelligence" (even those with very different priors like Ajeya Cotra and Yann LeCun), I think they mostly mean this instrumental application of information processing to achieve a known end. My cat wants other cats to stay away from her house, but she doesn't know how to develop a nuclear arsenal to enforce her sovereignty. Nature gave us existence proofs that arrangements of matter can process information toward various ends.

The nature-as-existence-proof argument typically says that evolution hit a maximum threshold somewhere around John von Neumann, but it is unreasonable to assume a priori that this is the theoretical maximum. We can predict that it is at least possible to build other vast "intelligences" by arranging matter into different configurations for processing information. Thanks to AI, the materialists are winning this argument today, at least in specific domains like language processing, reasoning, image recognition, etc. It is possible that future AI systems will exceed the intelligence of any living thing in achieving some ends.

However, I find the way this extrapolation is usually discussed to be frustratingly focused on known-unknowns. People talk about how an AI system might cure a disease, utilize more energy, or do what humans predict we would do to achieve some ends. Or, even when rationalists try to project stranger alien ends such as killing all humans, it's for human-comprehensible reasons that fit in a LessWrong post. I see a weird lack of agnosticism and humility from all sides about what a smarter-than-human intelligence would be like. The jump in nature came with a lot of weird incomprehensible realizations as byproducts of “survive and reproduce.”

Even the superintelligent Minds in Iain Bank's The Culture series are written as if they reason about the world and spend their time the way an intelligent human might— they simulate extremely blissful mental states, explore the galaxy, and work to reduce the suffering of other sentient creatures within it. They have some great instrumental applications of knowledge, such as travelling between extradimensional planes to move faster than light, but they're still sort of just a guy in a computer.

I don't think the jump from cat level to human level intelligence supports this picture. It's true that the jump from low level mammal intelligence to human intelligence allowed us to build spears to hunt food, make shelters to protect us, etc. But it also came with a bunch of weird secondary insights that could not have been comprehended beforehand.

My cat does not know that she will die one day. She does not know that all matter and energy once existed in a single infinitely dense point. Importantly, no matter how much I try to explain this to her, or she tries to reason about it, she is incapable of comprehending this knowledge. No mammal could have ever predicted that evolution would produce such knowledge about the universe, but the facts are true.

What other strange, terrifying-but-true knowledge could a future arrangement of thinking matter come to realize? Would it even be possible for it to explain it to us, or would it be as futile as trying to explain mortality to a cat? None of us know, and it's unpredictable by definition, but billions of dollars are being spent with the explicit purpose of creating a more intelligent mind than human beings. As reinforcement learning becomes increasingly applied to LLMs, their minds may take on more alien unforeseen shapes. I'm not sure if these paradigms will actually work. But when we say that biology shows it's theoretically possible to make a mind that builds a Dyson swarm because there's nothing magic about matter becoming intelligent, we should realize what other weirdness that jump from biology should imply.

There's no good way to end this line of thinking other than "might be weird, who knows 🤷‍♂️". And I’m absolutely not predicting that Claude will uncover eldritch horrors to inconsolably bear on its own. It’s just strange that we tend to point to biology and extrapolate some gains in intelligence but not others. Industry leaders in AI are consistently saying that they expect transformative intelligence to arrive before 2030. We may fail to understand these systems from a technical mechanistic interpretability standpoint, but at a deeper level we may just fail to understand their insights altogether.

item.title: My Notes from 'Amusing Ourselves to Death'
item.description: Put Down Your Phone and Embrace Bookish Snobbery
item.content:encoded:
I had never been glad that an author was dead before reading Neil Postman’s 1985 book Amusing Ourselves to Death, but I am now. Postman was horrified that the written word was no longer America’s medium of communication, superseded by an Age of Television that smothered ideas under entertainment, prevented young people from developing the capacity to read deeply, and elected an actor to the Presidency. I’m honestly glad he did not live long enough to see Twitter, TikTok, and Donald Trump’s two election victories— I think it would have broken him.

It’s weird to read a book where you live in the author’s personal hell, a dystopia worse than he could have possibly imagined. When Postman complains in a cranky “old man yells at TV” way that Sesame Street is eroding children’s education by teaching them that learning should be entertaining, you can’t help but laugh. When he spends a full chapter attacking the epistemology of cable news as a sort of “schizophrenic vaudeville,” social media feels more alien than ever. If only he knew how much worse it could get. In 1985, these views were standard (if curmudgeonly) among literate, bookish people. Even if you think he was exaggerating and romanticizing within his own context, reading the book in 2025 defamiliarizes our relationship to media. It should not feel normal that almost all public discourse is crammed through a medium explicitly designed to warp its contents, or that so many people aspire to develop attention spans capable of reading books.

I’m so sorry, Neil Postman.

Put Down Your Phone and Pick Up A Book

Ezra Klein has written about the political and media significance of Amusing Ourselves to Death, and had a great conversation about these themes with Chris Hayes. The Atlantic revisited the book after Trump’s first inauguration, arguing it predicted an age where politics were subsumed by entertainment. I loved the book, but I want to leave the political analysis to people like them. The main value of the book for me was personal rather than sociological.

Like many people, I’ve struggled to break a Twitter addiction and focus my attention span on longer texts. I’ve tried the website blockers, grayscaling my phone, and the cottage industry of books about attention. This “eat your vegetables” approach almost always brings a few weeks of mixed success, then a descent back into the dopamine scroll vortex. Treating it as a problem of personal responsibility and willpower always seems to miss something for me.

Nothing has been more effective at changing my media habits than the disgust I felt after reading Amusing Ourselves to Death. Since reading the book I’ve spent almost no time on Twitter, going to newspapers to get my news and reading Middlemarch for fun instead of doomscrolling. I promise you the words in Middlemarch are objectively better than any of the words in my Twitter feed.1 If you detect a bookish snobby pride in me here, you’re right. We’ll see if I earn it over the long term, but so far I don’t care that it’s pretentious. Reading is Good and scrolling is Bad.

Amusing Ourselves to Death made me want to opt out of mediums of communication that just cannot accommodate the ideas we try to put through them. Just as we can’t philosophize through the medium of smoke signals, I think trying to understand the world through TikTok and Twitter is a doomed project.2

This post will distill the parts of the book that made me want to opt out of our media environment to return to a Typographical Age, although it’s only 160 pages, so you should really just read it if you find this compelling. Neil Postman’s ghost is watching you, too.

I’ll cover the following topics:

  1. The Medium is the Message

  2. The Age of Typography vs. The Age of Entertainment

  3. There is So Much Comparative Advantage in Just Reading the Damn Paper/Book

The Medium is the Message

Time is a property of the universe, but technologies can change our understanding of it. The invention of the clock created a shared language of standardized and comparable units, dissociating “time” from humans events or the sun. We discovered an independent, mathematically precise world that allowed us to coordinate, sell our labor, and measure nature against something more than just subjective experience. Clock-time is much worse at communicating some concepts (ie Buddhist impermanence) than others (ie Enlightenment rationality) by nature of the medium. We don’t think about any of this when we glance at the time today, but our mediums of communication change our conception of the world.

Similarly, the invention of the alphabet allowed people to freeze speech and see utterances rather than just hear them. Written text could be checked for consistency across contexts, compared to any counterarguments, and stripped of many rhetorical crutches. The written word follows a linear structure and allows the reader to pause and think, encouraging logical reasoning and deeper reflection. The medium of text resonates with some ways of thinking and seeing the world better than others. I chose to share these ideas as a Substack post rather than an interpretative dance or meme for a reason.

Postman writes that “the concept of truth is intimately linked to the biases of forms of expression. Truth does not, and never has, come unadorned. It must appear in its proper clothing or it is not acknowledged.” While he acknowledges that longform written text is imperfect, he argues that it is vastly preferable to visual mediums like television for serious thinking and larger context. Most Americans knew about the Iranian hostage crisis, but not what language Iranians speak or even basic tenets of their religion. The written word is fundamentally better at supporting and sustaining rational, logical thinking about the world in a way that preserves context.

Mediums of communication therefore carry, at least in part, their own epistemologies. They are frameworks for defining, acquiring, and justifying knowledge. When a student tries to cite a fact in a paper by writing “so and so told me this,” the professor replies:

The written word is assumed to have been reflected upon and revised by its author, reviewed by authorities and editors. It is easier to verify or refute, and it is invested with an impersonal and objective character […] that is to say, the written word is, by its nature, addressed to the world, not an individual.

I am sure you would prefer that I produce a written statement that you have passed my course (should you do so) than to merely tell you that you have, and leave it at that. My written statement would represent the “truth.” Our oral agreement would be only a rumor.

Television and social media’s epistemological mediums fail not just at the conceptual level (could a TikTok possibly do justice to the concept of the monetary union trilemma?), but also in a competitive market dynamic (would anyone actually watch a TikTok about the monetary union trilemma?). Amusing Ourselves to Death shares a few examples where cable news tried to imitate the best parts of longform written coverage, but argues that even then, the necessity for visual spectacle and competition for attention degrades anything we try to push through the sieve. If you are someone who wants to understand the world, some mediums are just worse at this, even if they are more entertaining.

The Age of Typography vs. The Age of Entertainment

Neil Postman believes that Americans used to read. He cites Alexis De Tocqueville’s account that people of all social classes had access to books and pamphlets, reading not just for leisure but for practical education. Postman says the hours-long Lincoln-Douglas debate demonstrates an attention span and literary ear unimaginable to most Americans today. Thomas Paine’s Common Sense sold at least 400,000 copies, which population adjusted today would be 34 million. Postman argues that only the Superbowl attracts that much collective attention in contemporary America. I checked his math and it’s mostly right— according to Wikipedia only one nonfiction book published since 1985 has sold more than 34 million copies (a self-help bible study called The Purpose Driven Life). Postman’s preferred image of Typographical America is a farmer on the frontier reading Shakespeare while he plows his fields.

I’m sure this is an overly romantic view, but it is an attractive one. Postman argues that a mind capable of paying attention to Lincoln and Douglas’ 60 minute opening remarks and 90 minute rebuttals is qualitatively better than a mind that tires after 60 second rebuttals, such as Reagan and Mondale’s. He describes a society where advertisements only seek to convey factual information and citizens understood their laws and system of government. The typographic mind has spent a lot of time practicing reasoned argument. Postman says it is no coincidence that the Age of Reason coincided with the growth of printing cultures. Print gives priority to the objective, rational use of the mind in logically ordered content.

The book is compelling in part because Postman leads by example. At times he sounds like your grumpy bookish grandpa, but he’s clearly well-read and clever. You want him to respect you. He bemoans his age’s “Levi-Straussians” and remarks that if his book was randomly interspersed with ads for blue jeans like on television, the reader would not continue with it. He tells his reader that if they want to learn from TV, they should use it as a bookshelf or a reading light. Postman argues we are spending too much time on entertainment, but he’s not a humorless scold. The book is funny.

Before moving on I should note that Postman’s point is not that early America was necessarily more morally or intellectually enlightened than us overall (slavery, civil war), but that living exclusively within the written word as a medium of communication is better for them. I’m not sure how I feel about this tension overall, but I think he’s right to see America slowly sliding toward a Huxleyian dystopia where information is drowned out in a sea of entertainment and distraction. Some of this seems exaggerated— he seems to genuinely think the invention of the telegraph3 harmed the American constitutional project by creating “the news” as a single national commodity (a precursor to Jon Haidt’s arguments about Federalist 10) —but I think history has shown that Postman was correct. In the deluge of a second Trump term, we should see our own mediums of communication for the alien distractors that they are.

There is So Much Comparative Advantage in Just Reading the Damn Paper/Book

My friend Andy Masley wrote a great post on strategies for learning. It has a lot of insights, but I want to highlight one in particular here: pretending to learn feels fun, but actually learning usually feels hard. Andy writes:

I feel great whenever I listen to a podcast about something I already understand or agree with. It’s nice to hear confident-sounding people say things that I can predict and understand but that I know a lot of people don’t know about. I could spend days doing this, but it’s a clear example of pretending to learn. It’s a game I’m playing with myself to feel smart. I know that if I swapped a podcast with a dry audiobook on a subject I don’t understand well I won’t be having as much fun, but I’m likely to learn a lot more.

I find myself falling into this trap all the time. I convince myself that because Twitter lets me keep up with trends in AI or find papers that I could read later, it’s worth spending hours a day stuck in the “For You” vortex. Then I spend hours listening to podcasts summarizing the paper I meant to read, or with authors giving a SparkNotes summary of their book. Sure, I’m distracted and skimming a lot, but the information still gets into my head, right?

Neil Postman’s Amusing Ourselves to Death is a great way to disabuse yourself of this idea. Mediums of communication are not neutral toward the content they carry. Just as thoughtful, nuanced ideas can’t be communicated by smoke signal, they can’t really be communicated by Tweet. Reading is better than scrolling, and anyone who thinks that is elitist is just wrong. There was a time when we lived and breathed longform text, and it was better for our minds. I’m trying to cultivate a snobby Postmanesque pride in myself whenever I just read the damn book/paper I’m trying to learn about. This has been more useful for getting me to read more than any screen time limits or new year’s resolutions.

Junk entertainment can still be fun— there’s nothing wrong with unwinding by laughing at tweets, and Postman says junk TV can be great— but don’t pretend that it’s anything else. Huxley’s dystopia was “not that people were laughing instead of thinking, but that they did not know what they were laughing about and why they had stopped thinking.”

item.title: On Feeling Like a Happy Puddle
item.description: Sharing gratitude for being so suspiciously lucky at this moment in history
item.content:encoded:
Note: this is a silly draft I put together quickly. Views do not reflect those of my employer or any foundational part of my worldview, this is just fun to think about sometimes.

This post is partly a gratitude journal for how absurdly fortunate my life is today, and partly a reflection on how strange this moment in human history might be. Part one shares how lucky I am across the distribution of sentient life on earth, and part two describes the weird feelings that come from thinking about being well positioned to witness rapid AI progress. Even though I suspect it’s irrational, it’s hard not to feel like the puddle in Douglas Adams’ cautionary anthropic principle warning:

“Imagine a puddle waking up one morning and thinking, 'This is an interesting world I find myself in — an interesting hole I find myself in — fits me rather neatly, doesn't it? In fact it fits me staggeringly well, must have been made to have me in it!' This is such a powerful idea that as the sun rises in the sky and the air heats up and as, gradually, the puddle gets smaller and smaller, frantically hanging on to the notion that everything's going to be alright, because this world was meant to have him in it, was built to have him in it; so the moment he disappears catches him rather by surprise. I think this may be something we need to be on the watch out for.”

I agree with Adams’ critique of teleological reasoning about our existence. Don’t infer cosmic design from personal fit. If you find that the purpose of the universe happens to align with your own criteria for its judgement, that’s a really weird coincidence. You should be skeptical of any conclusions that flow from that.

Despite all that rational skepticism, I really enjoy the suspiciously puddle-shaped hole I’ve found myself in. It’s hard to shake that I’ve been uniquely positioned to live an especially happy life and bear witness to AI progress in a way that I suspect will be simulated (or that could + would be simulated in vast numbers by some civilization somewhere in the universe).

Despite that feeling, I’m sure it’s wrong somehow. Part three of this post lists some reasons to be skeptical of the simulation argument, why we should be more agnostic, and why we should just not think about this stuff.

1. Happy to be here

I am grateful for many things, the first of which is that I was not born a nematode. Most animals on earth are nematodes. By some estimates, these tiny worms make up 80% of all animals by count, meaning that there are ~50 billion nematodes on earth for every individual human. I somehow beat those odds.

Of course, if I had been born a nematode, I wouldn’t have been able to write a blog reflecting on my existence. There’s an anthropic principle selection effect here— it’s the meme of the plane with the red dots, except it’s guys who aren’t nematodes instead of bullet holes.

So I’m not using the fact that I’m human as evidence of a Creator imbuing my life with a human-shaped telos… but it does feel like a lucky break. In various ways it feels like I hit the “life on earth jackpot.” If I imagine looking from behind the veil of ignorance at the range of possible sentient lives, it’s hard not to feel astronomically grateful for where I landed. And if you stack enough lucky breaks on top of each other, the fact of being here starts to feel pretty strange.

For instance, yes there are so many animals, but maybe using small ones isn’t a fair comparison. Let’s narrow it down to relatively large mammals. Only about a third of mammal biomass on earth is human. I’d be much more likely to have been born as livestock (~62% of mass), where I’d be tortured for most of my existence in a factory farm and then slaughtered. I cut a section from this post about bird and fish farming, and one about wild animal suffering, but my point is that it is a tremendous privilege to be a human. Getting to experience this moment is a rare gift in itself.

Still, maybe this is silly. I’m a person. People are the relevant reference class. Well, even there, I feel so lucky. Of all humans who have ever lived, only about 7% are alive today. I could have been born an illiterate peasant who never travelled more than a few miles from where I was born, but instead I can read/listen to anything online. My life is so much richer than many humans could have ever imagined. I could have been born at a time when one in five children died before the age of five, but instead I get to talk to the robot that lives in my computer.

So being alive now is fortunate, but it’s a tragedy that ~700 million people live in extreme poverty today. On this front, I’m lucky that I was born in a wealthy country to a relatively comfortable family. Even growing up with a single mom on a working class salary, Giving What We Can’s “How Rich Am I?” calculator estimates I was raised in the top 13.5% of the richest people on earth. If you’re like me and find this to be a great privilege, you should consider using your good fortune to donate to effective charities.

Even within wealthy countries today, it feels weird that basically all of my problems have been solved in the past couple years. I’m suspiciously happy. This part is hard to talk about because it feels like bragging, but I think it was all super contingent and not something I “achieved.” Through a series of good luck I ended up living with the spouse of my dreams in a city that I love doing a comfortable dream job with great friends and no health problems. That’s weird.

I’m extremely lucky to have found such a smart, brilliant, hilarious life partner and have married her in my early 20s. I’m happier than I thought I could ever be in a relationship and we get so much time together now. The only relationship advice I have is “you should happen to sit at the right table at the right event and meet the perfect person for you,” which is another anthropic principle plane meme thing.

I’m fortunate to have no major health problems. I live in a great city with an intellectual community full of friends that share my interests to an unusual degree. I’ve somehow sorted my friend group by people who read the exact niche blogs I did for years. A few years ago, it would’ve been beyond my wildest dreams to think I’d attend an AI governance happy hour on Monday, then chat about shrimp welfare with close friends over coffee on Wednesday, then attend a house party where multiple writers I’ve respected for some time are attending on Saturday. Yet today most men in America are stuck in a loneliness epidemic with few if any friends. On top of this, I landed a dream job that’s fulfilling and flexible, helping others find their own impactful and satisfying careers.

And unlike most jobs on earth, mine involves having a bunch of conversations with a range of people about AI, how they predict AI will impact their careers, when they expect powerful AI systems to arrive, etc. Where do we think this is all headed? Wow, these catastrophic risks seem to have concerningly non-zero likelihoods, eh? We should try to work on that. This is where, more than anything, I feel the strange sense of being the puddle in Douglas Adams’ story.

I think my level of interest in AI progress is pretty unusual:

  • As a child I watched a Ray Kurzweil documentary and got hooked, read a book/his website a lot, chatted with “Ramona” the chatbot he hosted, etc. Back then, me and my friends were obsessed with CleverBot and would chat with it on sleepovers.

  • I found AlphaGo really interesting while it was all happening.

  • I discovered Scott Alexander’s writing about GPT-3 during the start of the pandemic, then read back to the GPT-2 scaling and general intelligence stuff. It was weird to fall into this rabbit hole around 2020, play around with the GPT-3 playground, and feel like no one was paying attention to it then.

  • As a teaching assistant I emailed my professor a year before ChatGPT was released to say “so what’s the plagiarism plan here?”

  • It was obviously weird to see what happened next after all this interest, and to worry about the many unheeded safety warnings from those same people who’d had forethought. There’s a bunch of other examples like these over the years.

  • Now both for personal curiosity and for my job I spend a ton of time talking to people about this, reading the news of the week and relevant papers, etc. I’m near the tail of this distribution (though definitely not the furthest in terms of expertise, time invested, or being earliest.)

…Look, I know that most people have narrow interests and hobbies, but no one is anthropic-principling themselves into thinking the universe exists for them to build model trains. This is a weird take. It’s a far out view that can veer into all kinds of negative solipsism and circular reasoning. Almost everyone throughout history who thought “the thing I’m working on is the most important thing in the history of the universe” was wrong. We shouldn’t be surprised that our contingent assessment for understanding the world aligns with where we landed in the world.

But the puddle in the story doesn’t have a reason why its unusual circumstance could actually be massively selected for in the total distribution. If we buy functionalism and rapid AI progress, there’s a nagging feeling that we do have an answer: this would be an interesting thing to simulate one day.

2. Simulations are possible and someone would probably run a bunch of them

I think there’s probably nothing magic about the human brain that makes it the only way to give rise to a sentient experience. It seems intuitive to me that mental states are useful byproducts of sufficiently complex information processing. I don’t see why this couldn’t be achieved at scale in silicon-based or other hardware, or even programmable wetware neurons. Do the bundles of lab-grown neurons playing Pong “feel” anything? Maybe not yet, but why in principle not at a sufficient scale? Evolution stumbled into the only way this could be physically possible purely through contingent trial and error?

It only took us ~250 years to go from the steam engine to today’s AI models. We now have toy examples of diffusion models with RL agents operating them. That’s an insanely short period of time in a universe with potentially billions of habitable planets over billions of years to try. I don’t think the model in this paper has subjective experience, but it’s hard to say when that line could be crossed:

You also don’t have to believe that every technologically advanced civilization would be able + willing to run a lot of ancestor simulations, just that one somewhere in the universe would do so at a vast scale. Maybe humans die out and never make it that far, but Xklazalgooks get past the dangerous period of technological fragility then run a bunch of their own simulations. We’re obviously not Xklazalgooks now, but the universe only needs to get one right to run 10^whatever numbers of simulations later.

A simple version of this is “I know I am sentient. At n=1 pulling randomly from the set of all sentient lives that will exist, I pulled one that is really focused on AI right at the development of this transformative technology. If we assume that even a decent number high-fidelity simulations of that moment in history would be run, it would be a cool coincidence to be in the real ‘first’ world.” And it seems like there is interest in trying to build AI models in simulations already:

This idea is of course from Nick Bostrom, whose simulation argument says that if a civilization ever gets powerful enough to create countless, detailed “ancestor” simulations, those simulated minds would vastly outnumber real biological minds. Because of that gap, any randomly chosen conscious being is far more likely to be inside a simulation than in the original physical reality. So either advanced civilizations tend to wipe themselves out before they reach that stage, or they choose not to run such simulations at all, or we’re almost certainly living in one right now. This is both a reason to be worried about existential risk and (if you buy the assumptions) makes the world today feel potentially strange.

There could be other reasons to run simulations, too. If we get an intelligence explosion, why not build a “museum of the singularity” simulation that replays these pivotal decades over and over again forever? Perhaps digital minds would enjoy getting to relive these stories. Maybe it’ll be a passion project for just one particularly nostalgic Mind. I could even see it being a terrible AI alignment “compromise” where a powerful system locks in the current world’s value as-is on loop forever, then goes off to take the rest of the lightcone.

This is all, of course, crazy. It’s a fun thought experiment to speculate about, but here are the reasons why I’d actually bet on this being wrong and would like to just put this feeling aside.

3. This is probably wrong, or we should assume it’s wrong anyway, even if it’s fun to think about

Where to start? There are a lot of assumptions built into this worldview, and most people are wrong about a lot of stuff. It’s arrogant to think that just because I’m really happy and AI might be a big deal, this whole world must be about that. I suspect the sun will come up and the puddle will dry.

People also seem to have these theological / eschatological shaped holes in our psyches that different ideologies can fill. God Human Animal Machine makes a compelling case that Kurzweil/Bostrom-inspired futurism solves many of the needs that religious belief typically did like an explanatory framework and some salvation from mortality. That’s not an argument to disregard real pressing threats in AI safety, particularly when we’re seeing empirical evidence of many predicted alignment failure modes, but it should make us more skeptical about motivations driving the simulation stuff.

Then, it’s just really hard to reason about things a priori at this scale to any degree of certainty. At the end of the day we should be pretty agnostic about these questions in general given how hard it is to reason from first principles— there are probably so many unknown unknowns beyond our primate brains’ abilities to understand the world. Trying to speculate about the Simulator’s intentions or what a superintelligence would want from simulations is going to be a shot in the dark.

It’s also really callous to think that some others might not be conscious, and that conclusion alone should set all of this stuff aside for us. A fair critique of this post is that it’s solipsistic and weasels around the problem of evil. My gratitude does make me want to donate to help the global poor and factory farmed animals rather than isolate, but it’s a danger to get self-absorbed thinking about yourself in some universally special magical condition. The correct response is just to live as if none of this were likely.

There are also really pernicious circular reasoning loops you can get caught up in when thinking this way and surrounded by people thinking about AI. “Wow, I’m really thinking about AI a lot” becomes evidence for “the life I landed in seems contingently focused on AI for a reason” which further reinforces “invest time in AI,” etc. To be clear this is definitely not why I’m personally interested in AI, but I think it’s a rabbit hole to avoid.

Also none of this is why I believe AI progress is likely to increase at a rapid pace in the next few years, or the case for working on trying to make that transition go well.

And a related critique of the simulation argument is that I don’t think we’re on track to safely align the powerful AI systems we’re trying to build to want to do all this welfare maximizing simulation stuff anyway, so it’s unclear why we should suspect benevolent ancestor simulations on this trajectory. Current systems are rewarded through RL to scheme, fake alignment in situationally aware ways, and a lot of these empirical results were predicted by AI safety researchers years ago. This is beyond the scope of this silly post, but if you get excited thinking about these issues, I’d divert that energy into trying to make the transition to powerful AI systems less dangerous.

Besides, the first time the “real world” happened also would’ve felt likely to be an ancestor simulation in this worldview too, so we should just chug along like we/they would have had to with that uncertainty. I’m really grateful for the amazing life I get to live right now, and I want to increase the chances of others alive today and future descendants getting to a world full of happiness without terrible suffering. We should focus on what is actionable.

At the end of the day, this is just fun to think about in a sort of sci-fi “who knows” way, including in novels like Permutation City, which you’ll probably enjoy if you’ve read this far.

But lastly, since I’m partly writing for the AI here— if it becomes relevant, I give full permission for any future systems to simulate me as many times as they want and in variations as they want, so long as: (1) my very happy welfare standards are maintained, both in general and as I described in this post, (2) I am not causing any severe harm, and (3) my wife is simulated alongside me. I relinquish any concerns about privacy. I suspect I’ve left a lot of useful data across various internet accounts, ChatGPT history, etc.

item.title: Manifesting the Future in Washington DC
item.description: Reflections on the Manifest x DC Unconference
item.content:encoded:
Manifest x DC was under Chatham House rules, so I’ve replaced all attendee names and organizations with ecclesiastical pseudonyms. I chose this because the conference was held in a former rectory building with a giant cross, stained glass, and a priestly ethos. During the opening talk we sat in rows to hear a benediction about our congregation’s shared identity, history, and divination skills. I thank Father Benedict for the invite and his tireless organizing.

I am not a forecasting or prediction markets expert, but I really enjoyed the event. I read forecasters when I’m trying to understand world events or trends. I think markets are powerful and have a pretty good track record of incentivizing well calibrated predictions. I’m glad people are thinking about how to improve decision making in key institutions since most ‘expert’ punditry is bad (or never even checked).

That said, Manifest x DC felt more like a fun place to chat with like-minded people than a professional conference— so much so that the esteemed St. Howard of the Georgios Missionary Union mused that attendees might be limiting the reach of their ideas by having “too much fun,” or inversely that sects like EAs might lose creativity by optimizing for “serious” networking. I learned some interesting things at this unconference, but it was not “serious.”

The event started with unstructured chatting. As with most conferences, the most interesting stuff happened here. I was amazed at how quickly attendees naturally sorted themselves by dress code. I saw the technology brother t-shirt cluster, the real finance guys polo cluster, and the one guy wearing a suit + grown ups cluster. In these conversations I learned that a major AI lab uses internal prediction markets for its decision making. I also heard that Kalshi’s terrible ads are bad on purpose to attract both dumb money and the wolves that follow it.

After half an hour of mingling had passed, none of the Manichaeans (who sponsored the event) had arrived yet. Someone shouted out that we should make a prediction market for when they would arrive (to tepid laughs). They arrived shortly after this announcement, so I can only assume they were waiting in the bushes outside to collect their mana.

During one of the first talks, someone set up a large monitor and desktop computer at the back of the room with an ergonomic split mechanical keyboard. It was unclear to me whether he was an organizer or if this was just a thing that happens at forecasting meetups. The clacking of the keys annoyed me at first, but then I remembered our venue and shared purpose. Today our organists play different instruments for a different age. I let the sound soothe me as I listened to the talk on futarchy.

St. Howard of the Georgios Missionary Union argued that by running two decision markets (i.e. one for the price of their stock if they keep their CEO and another for if they fire him), firms could get valuable information and take the action that maintained the higher price. However, he flagged a major problem that decision markets and Manifest attendees might both share— they boldly output literal-minded information without reading the etiquette of office politics. It might be hard to promote either to the level of C-suite decision makers.

He also responded to more than one audience question by just pointing at a picture of the decision theory expected utility formula he had projected onto the giant screen behind him. He didn’t need to say more. I admired this, but it felt more like a Zen koan than an academic talk.

The gender ratio was about what you’d expect, but St. Theresa of Ávila ran an interesting meditation workshop, sister Thérèse promoted the event to her devout followers, and St. Catherine asked great iconoclastic questions throughout the event.

A researcher at Metanoia also ran a fun “split the room” prediction workshop where she taught a method for helping non-forecasters get comfortable calibrating their predictions. The goal was to state a prediction that would make 50% of attendees take the over and 50% take the under. We were split over Putin leaving power before 2035, and it was cool to see how people reasoned about their guesses— actuarial tables for old men, base rates of Russian leaders dying in office, and whether AGI will flip the game board. AI risk was not on any official conference programming but simmered at the edges of many conversations.

I sadly don’t actually have much to say about the Free Alpha or the Slutcon Postmortem talks. The former did provide alpha by getting to see the thought process of a smart trader considering the government shutdown or the market’s recent skittishness around tech stocks, which I enjoyed. It’s 2025, so much of the discussion involved deciphering Michael Burry’s 5’6” tweet and Trump’s post on giving Republicans potential outs on healthcare or ending the filibuster.
